title: Core Security Concepts
lead: Threat, vulnerability, exploit, and mitigation; attack types, security program elements, and the principles that everything else in the domain builds on.

head: Term
What it is
Example
rows: an unpatched service, a default password
an attacker, malware, an insider, a fire
a specific way to take advantage of a vulnerability
a script that exploits a CVE
a patch, an ACL, segmentation, training

blocks.text: Exam wording almost always tests exactly this distinction: "a vulnerability is a weakness in the system," "a threat is something that could take advantage of it."

The **CIA** triad: **confidentiality** (only authorized parties can see the data), **integrity** (data isn't changed without detection), **availability** (the service works when it's needed). Every mitigation protects one of these three; every attack violates one.

head: Attack
What it does
Mitigated by
rows: forges an address (IP, MAC, ARP, DHCP)
DAI, DHCP snooping, uRPF, port security
inserts itself into someone else's exchange
password policy, MFA, lockout after N attempts

blocks.title: Remember
paras: No technical control stops social engineering — the correct answer to these questions is always **user awareness training**.

blocks.text: The exam expects you to distinguish three elements:

items: **User awareness** — general awareness: mailers, posters, simulated phishing emails. The goal is for an employee to recognize a threat.
**Training** — targeted skill-building: how to use a VPN, how to handle data. Usually paired with a knowledge check.
**Physical access control** — locks, badge readers, restricted-access server rooms, video surveillance. Everything else is pointless if someone can walk up to a device and plug in a console cable.

sections.title: Principles the concrete settings grow out of

items: **Defense in depth** — several independent layers: perimeter, segmentation, host protection, access control. One breached layer doesn't open everything.
**Least privilege** — exactly as much access as the job requires, no more.
**Separation of duties** — critical actions require two roles.
**AAA** — who you are (authentication), what you're allowed to do (authorization), what you did (accounting).
**Patching and inventory** — you can't protect what you don't know about.

sections.title: Devices that separate networks by trust

blocks.text: This role is covered in detail in the network components chapter, but the exam also asks about it separately within the security domain — keep the short version handy:

items: **Firewall** — a device that **permits or blocks traffic between segments of different trust levels** (internal network ↔ internet, internal network ↔ DMZ), deciding by policy what's allowed and what isn't. That exact phrasing — "determines which packets are allowed to cross from unsecured to secured networks" — is the correct answer to a question about a firewall's role, not "blocks all traffic" and not "acts as a default gateway."

**Stateful inspection** — a firewall remembers established sessions and lets return traffic through automatically, without a separate rule for each direction (unlike an ACL, which evaluates every packet independently — more on that in the ACL chapter).

A firewall is a device that **segregates a network into zones with their own policy** (the same idea in other words: "segregates a network into separate zones," "separates networks by security domains"), and by doing so **protects the internal network from the internet**.

**Proxy / Web Security Appliance (WSA)** — an intermediary for web requests: it caches content (faster repeat access) and filters by site reputation/category. Caching speeds up **web traffic specifically**, not the network as a whole.

blocks.text: **MFA** means two or more **different** factors. A password plus a security question is still one factor (both are "knowledge"), and that option is wrong wherever it appears as an answer choice.
**Certificates** and **biometrics** show up as stronger alternatives to a password: a certificate can't be brute-forced, and biometrics can't be forgotten.
The rest of the domain's chapters are concrete implementations of these principles:

items: passwords and device access — [least privilege applied to the hardware itself];
ACLs — filtering traffic by policy;
Layer 2 security — protecting against spoofing inside a segment;
AAA — centralized authentication;
VPN and IPsec — confidentiality and integrity over an untrusted link;
wireless security — the same problem over the air, where the medium is open to everyone.

sections.title: Incident walkthrough: naming each element correctly

blocks.text: Scenario: a web application on a server has a known, unpatched file-upload handling bug (the CVE was published six months ago). An attacker finds the server by scanning the internet, runs a publicly available script against that CVE, uploads a web shell, and gains access to the database. The administrator applies the patch and adds a WAF rule.
Breaking this down using the terms from the first table:

items: **Vulnerability** — the unpatched file-upload handling bug itself; it existed before the attack, regardless of whether anyone ever used it.
**Threat** — the attacker as a potential source of harm (more broadly, anyone who could scan the internet and find the vulnerable server).
**Exploit** — the specific script that takes advantage of this vulnerability to upload the web shell; without the exploit, the vulnerability would have stayed theoretical.
**Mitigation** — the patch and the WAF rule put in place after the incident.

blocks.title: Trap
paras: "Vulnerability" and "exploit" get mixed up most often in this direction: a vulnerability is a **property of the system** (it exists whether or not anyone attacks it), an exploit is an **action or tool** that uses it. The question "what takes advantage of a vulnerability" is asking about the exploit — not the threat, not the vulnerability itself.

sections.title: Walkthrough: which side of the CIA triad each attack violates

blocks.text: Attacks don't hit all three sides of the triad equally — the exam likes to test exactly this mapping:

head: Attack
Primary CIA impact
Why
rows: the service is unreachable for legitimate users; data is neither stolen nor altered
an outsider reads the data; the data itself is unchanged
Routing table spoofing / MITM with on-the-fly packet modification
the receiver sees something different from what the source sent
files are encrypted (altered) and simultaneously unavailable to the owner
an outsider read data they should never have seen

blocks.title: Remember
paras: A single attack can hit more than one side of the triad at once (ransomware is the canonical example), but on a single-answer question look for the **primary, most direct** effect: for DDoS that's always availability, even though the remote service is also temporarily unreachable for legitimate read requests.

sections.title: Diagnosis: telling a targeted attack apart from an organic traffic spike

blocks.text: **Symptom.** An online store's server suddenly stops responding; the link is saturated.
**What to look at.** The character of the sources and content, not just the volume:

items: **Legitimate spike** (a sale, a post going viral) — sources are geographically diverse but match the profile of ordinary customers: varied User-Agent strings, meaningful catalog queries, behavior patterns that look like real shoppers, and a new-vs-returning visitor ratio typical of marketing activity.

**DDoS** — sources are either abnormally uniform (the same low-effort request from thousands of different addresses — a classic botnet signature) or clearly spoofed IPs that don't correspond to any real member of the site's audience; the requests don't behave like real users (no loading of images and stylesheets after the HTML, no pause to "read" the page).

blocks.text: **Conclusion.** The difference isn't in the number of requests per second — it's in their **nature**. That's the exam takeaway: a DDoS attack looks like overload from the network's point of view, but you diagnose it by the mismatch between the traffic and real user behavior, not by a load metric. The mitigation differs too: an organic spike is fixed by scaling infrastructure, while DDoS is fixed with filtering and rate limiting at the edge, often with help from a provider or a dedicated traffic-scrubbing service.

items: "What is the difference between a vulnerability and an exploit?" — a weakness versus a way to take advantage of it.
"Which element of a security program teaches users to recognise phishing?" — user awareness / training.
"Which two are examples of multifactor authentication?" — password + token, password + fingerprint; two passwords does not count.
"Which attack intercepts traffic between two hosts?" — man-in-the-middle.
"What mitigates social engineering?" — user training.
"What is the principle of least privilege?" — the minimum access necessary to do the job.
"Which component of the CIA triad is primarily affected by a DDoS attack?" — availability.
"An attacker modifies data in transit without the sender or receiver noticing. Which CIA principle is violated?" — integrity.

"Ransomware encrypts a company's files and demands payment. Which two CIA principles does this attack affect?" — integrity (files are altered/encrypted) and availability (the owner can no longer use them).
"What takes advantage of a vulnerability to compromise a system?" — an exploit, not a threat and not the vulnerability itself.
"What distinguishes a DDoS attack from a legitimate traffic spike?" — not the traffic volume itself, but its nature: uniform requests, spoofed sources, behavior that doesn't match real users.

items.q: An unpatched vulnerability in a web server, a script to exploit it, and an attacker — name each one correctly.
Password plus a security question — is that MFA?
items.a: No, both belong to the "knowledge" factor; a second factor of a different type is required.

items.q: What mitigates a rogue DHCP server on a segment?
items.a: DHCP snooping — trusted ports for the real server, everything else on untrusted ports is dropped.

items.q: What does defense in depth mean?
items.a: Several independent layers of protection, so a failure in one doesn't open access to everything.

items.q: What are the three components of the CIA triad?
A company's unpatched server is hit by a known, publicly available CVE script. What's the exploit here, and what's the vulnerability?
items.a: The vulnerability is the unpatched bug on the server itself (it existed before the attack); the exploit is the specific script that uses it to break in.

items.q: A DDoS attack overwhelms a website. Which side of the CIA triad does it violate first?
items.a: Availability — the service is unreachable for legitimate users, while data is neither stolen nor altered.

items.q: Ransomware encrypted a company's files. One side of the CIA triad, or two?
items.a: Two: integrity (files altered by encryption) and availability (the owner can't use them), simultaneously.

items.q: Traffic to a site spikes sharply. How do you tell a DDoS apart from an organic spike without looking at requests per second?
items.a: By the nature of the traffic: uniform, meaningless requests from thousands of addresses or clearly spoofed sources point to DDoS; diverse behavior that looks like real shoppers points to an organic spike.
